summary: Collects in one place the syntax (ABNF) changes that many IMAP extensions made to base IMAP commands from RFC 3501. It also suggests patterns for adding options to existing commands so future extensions stay compatible. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Many people added new words to the same language over the years. This puts all the new grammar rules on one page.

questions: how do imap extensions add options to commands
subtitle: One place for the grammar of IMAP command extensions, plus a standard pattern for adding new options.

tldr.problem: Over the years many IMAP extensions added syntax to the base commands in RFC 3501, and each one described its change in its own document in its own style.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4466 collects the ABNF for these changes in one place and gives SELECT, EXAMINE, CREATE, RENAME, FETCH, STORE and SEARCH the same optional-parameter shape, built on a generic tagged-ext syntax.
tldr.outcome: Future extensions can plug into existing commands in a compatible way. The RFC changes no semantics, only syntax, and it has since been updated by RFC 6237 and RFC 7377.

facts.label: Commands extended
facts.value: SELECT, EXAMINE, CREATE, RENAME, FETCH, STORE, SEARCH, APPEND

today: RFC 4466 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 6237 and RFC 7377. The RFC itself says its ABNF is expected to be folded into a future revision of RFC 3501.

sections.title: Why Collect the Grammar
sections.content:
Documents from the IMAPEXT and LEMONADE working groups, and many individual documents, had added syntax to the base IMAP commands described in RFC 3501. RFC 4466 pulls most of those ABNF changes into one document so that readers do not have to chase cross references.

It has three stated purposes: rationalize and generalize the ABNF of some existing extensions, collect it in one place, and define building blocks that future extensions can use together. It updates the ABNF in RFCs 2088, 2342, 3501, 3502 and 3516, and includes part of the errata to RFC 3501.

It does not specify any semantic changes to those RFCs. The text also says it is expected that a future revision will be folded into a revision of RFC 3501.
sections.eli5: People kept adding new rules to a game, each on a different scrap of paper. This RFC puts all the rules on one page without changing how the game is played.

sections.title: The Tagged Extension Pattern
sections.content:
The core of the design is a generic syntax called tagged-ext: a label followed by a value. A tagged-ext-label starts with a letter, a hyphen, an underscore or a period, and may continue with those characters plus digits and the colon. It is always a valid RFC 3501 atom.

A tagged-ext-val is either a simple value (a sequence-set or a number) or a parenthesized list of components, which can be nested. Where a mandatory value is always a number or a sequence-set, the enclosing parentheses are not needed.

The RFC marks this as the recommended syntax for future extensions. Where the extension might use a nullable string, it says to use nstring instead of astring, and that a URL should be represented as a quoted string.

Because every extension has the same shape, a parser can recognise a parameter's name and skip or reject its value without knowing what it means.
sections.eli5: Every new feature has to arrive wearing the same kind of name tag followed by its gift. That way the receiver can read the tag even if it has never seen the gift before.

sections.title: Commands That Gain Extension Points
sections.content:
Section 2 of the RFC (which it calls not normative) describes where options now go. SELECT and EXAMINE accept a parenthesized list of attribute/value parameters after the mailbox name. CREATE takes them after the mailbox name and RENAME after the new mailbox name. FETCH and UID FETCH gain optional fetch modifiers, and STORE and UID STORE gain optional store modifiers.

The same rules apply everywhere. The order of parameters is arbitrary, a value is optional, and a value that is present appears in parentheses. Any parameter or modifier that the server does not support as an extension must be rejected with a BAD response. For example, a SELECT INBOX (BLURDYBLOOP) gets a BAD Unknown parameter in SELECT command.

For SELECT and EXAMINE there are two modes. A parameter may cause a global state change that lasts for the session, or a per-mailbox change that lasts only while that mailbox is selected. This document itself defines no CREATE parameters, no RENAME parameters, no fetch modifiers and no store modifiers.
sections.eli5: Each command gets a little pocket for extras. If you put something in the pocket that the server has never heard of, the server says no.

sections.title: Extended SEARCH and ESEARCH
sections.content:
SEARCH is extended with optional result options, written as RETURN (...) before the search program. No result options are defined here. Options may carry parameters in parentheses, and unsupported options must be rejected with BAD.

The RFC also defines a new untagged ESEARCH response meant as a better version of the SEARCH response. It SHOULD be sent as the result of an extended SEARCH or UID SEARCH. For a given extended command the SEARCH and ESEARCH responses SHOULD be mutually exclusive.

An ESEARCH response has an optional search correlator holding the tag of the command that caused it, an optional UID indicator (if present, all data refers to UIDs, otherwise to message numbers), and then one or more name/value pairs that may come in any order. Unless an extension says otherwise, a return item name SHOULD appear only once.
sections.eli5: The old search answer was a plain list. The new one is a labelled answer sheet, such as how many matches there were and which ones, so new kinds of answers can be added later.

sections.title: APPEND and Existing Extensions
sections.content:
APPEND is handled slightly differently so that existing extensions keep working. The BINARY extension lets a client append data containing NULs using the literal8 syntax, and MULTIAPPEND lets a client append several messages atomically. RFC 4466 defines one common APPEND syntax that takes both into account, and does not change the meaning of either extension.

The literal8 non-terminal is extended so that a non-synchronizing literal (a trailing +) is allowed when the server supports both BINARY and LITERAL+. Only a single append-message may appear when MULTIAPPEND is not present.

The ABNF in section 6 of RFC 2342 (Namespace) was rewritten to conform to the ABNF of RFC 4234 and restructured for readability. The RFC states there were no changes on the wire. It also redefines status-att-list from RFC 3501 so that STATUS extensions can extend one production.
sections.eli5: When the new pocket would have broken an older trick, the authors built a slightly different pocket so that the older trick still works.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The documents that RFC 4466 updates must still be consulted for the security considerations of their own extensions. The new concern is parser complexity: as a protocol gets more complex, parser bugs such as buffer overflows and denial of service become more common. The RFC says that to the extent it makes the parser more consistent and so simpler, the situation improves, and the impact depends on how many deployed extensions follow it.

Commands allowed in the NOT AUTHENTICATED state are more sensitive because the attacker community is larger before authentication and some servers run with elevated privileges then. This document extends no such commands, and future extensions to them should favor simplicity over consistency or extensibility.
sections.eli5: The more complicated the reading rules, the more chances to misread. Keeping the rules the same everywhere helps, and the doors open to strangers should have the simplest rules of all.
